summary: Orbit Health is a web app that turns astronaut health data into something a crew member can understand at a glance. It shows an interactive 3D body where each organ is color-coded depending on its status. It matters because crews far from Earth must monitor themselves with limited medical support.
details:
Orbit Health is a web app that shows an astronaut how their body is coping with spaceflight. At its centre is an interactive 3D human body. Each tracked organ has its own colour and glows green (normal), amber (watch) or pulsing red (act now). Clicking an organ gives a plain-language explanation, likely causes and recommended actions.

Status comes from four sources:

  • A daily check-in covering heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise and radiation dose. Each person is compared with their own baseline, built from their first check-ins, and not with a generic range.
  • A simulated live sensor feed with heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing, temperature, blood pressure, cabin CO2 and a radiation dosimeter. Scenarios such as exercise, sleep, rising CO2 and a solar particle event show how the signals and organ colours react.
  • Nutrition and physical-activity tracking (calories, fluids, calcium, vitamin D, aerobic and resistance training).
  • Live NASA and NOAA data. NASA DONKI space-weather events raise the status of radiation-sensitive organs. JPL Horizons gives Moon and Mars distance and communication delay. NASA OSDR/GeneLab links organs to space-biology studies. NASA APOD provides a daily image, and NOAA SWPC provides the solar-cycle phase.

Gamification (XP, levels, streaks, daily missions and badges) rewards the habits that protect health in space. The astronaut profile chooses the female or male anatomy model.

Benefits and intended impact

Crews far from Earth have limited medical support and long communication delays, so they need to understand their own health quickly. Orbit Health turns raw numbers into clear, personal, space-weather-aware guidance. We hope it helps people spot problems early and stay motivated. The same approach could support remote clinics, polar stations and other places far from care.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules).
  • three.js for the 3D viewer.
  • Open Anatomy 3D models, based on BodyParts3D (CC BY 4.0).
  • Node.js, Express and Firebase (authentication and database) in the full version.
  • A static GitHub Pages version for judging, with no login. Its backend logic runs in the browser and data is saved in each visitor’s own browser.
  • NASA APIs (DONKI, APOD, OSDR/GeneLab, JPL Horizons) and NOAA SWPC.

Creativity

We combined real space-weather data with a personal baseline and a colour-coded 3D body, so one glance shows how space is affecting each organ. Game elements and animation make daily self-monitoring something people want to do.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: the sensor feed is simulated, and the app says so. If a live data source is unavailable, it shows a message instead of invented values.
  • Not medical advice: targets and thresholds are simplified and illustrative.
  • Privacy: the judge version is anonymous and collects no personal data.
  • Accessibility and clarity: plain language, colour plus text labels, and reduced-motion support.
  • Attribution: anatomy credits and data sources are shown in the app.
